m2s1p1: A solar panel is built from many small photovoltaic (PV) cells. Each cell is a thin slice of semiconductor material — most commonly crystalline silicon — treated to have two distinct layers: a negatively-charged n-type layer on top and a positively-charged p-type layer below. The interface between these layers is called the p-n junction.
m2s1p2: When a photon of light strikes the cell with enough energy, it knocks an electron loose from the silicon lattice. The built-in electric field at the p-n junction pushes the free electron toward the n-type side and the corresponding "hole" toward the p-type side, creating a voltage that drives current through an external circuit.
m2step1p: A photon from the sun strikes the silicon surface. If its energy exceeds the bandgap (~1.1 eV for silicon), it excites an electron to the conduction band.
m2step2p: The built-in electric field at the p-n junction sweeps the free electron to the n-side and the hole to the p-side, preventing immediate recombination.
m2step3p: Metal contacts on the front (thin grid lines) and rear (full sheet) collect the electrons. The front grid is designed to minimise shading.
m2step4p: Electrons flow out through the front contacts, through your load and back in through the rear contact — that's usable DC electricity.
m2step5p: Individual cells are wired in series strings, encapsulated in EVA polymer, sandwiched between tempered glass and a backsheet, and framed in aluminium.
m2s3p1: Not all solar panels are the same. The three main commercial technologies differ in efficiency, cost, appearance and best use case.
m2monoNote: Best efficiency, uniform black look, ideal for limited roof space.
m2polyNote: Blue speckled look, lower cost, slightly lower efficiency than mono.
m2thinNote: Flexible, performs better in high heat & low light, lower efficiency.
m2s4Title: Why real output is lower than the rating
m2s4p1: The nameplate wattage assumes Standard Test Conditions. In practice, several factors reduce output.
m2s4callout: Temperature coefficient. Silicon panels lose roughly 0.35–0.5 % of power per °C above 25 °C. On a hot roof (65 °C cell temp), output drops ~14–20 % vs the STC rating.
m2tblN1: Higher cell temp → lower Voc and power
m2tblN2: Even partial shading on one cell affects the whole string
m2tblN3: Worse in arid climates; regular cleaning helps
m2tblN4: Use correct cable gauge to minimise resistance
m2tblN6: Panels lose ~0.5 % output per year (LID + aging)
m2s5Title: Key electrical parameters on the datasheet
m2s5p1: Every panel ships with a datasheet. Knowing what each parameter means lets you size wiring, inverters and charge controllers correctly.
m2s5li1: Pmax (Wp) — Peak power at STC. Example: 400 Wp.
m2s5li2: Voc — Open-circuit voltage. Used to size inverter input and avoid over-voltage.
m2s5li3: Vmp — Voltage at maximum power point. Typically ~80 % of Voc.
m2s5li4: Isc — Short-circuit current. Used to size fuses and wiring.
m2s5li5: Imp — Current at maximum power point. Pmax = Vmp × Imp.
m2s5li6: η (eta) — Efficiency. Ratio of electrical output to incident solar power × panel area.
m2s5callout: Design tip. Always use Voc (not Vmp) when checking the maximum input voltage of your inverter or charge controller.
m2q1text: What creates the voltage in a solar cell?
m2q1a: Heat from the sun warming the metal contacts
m2q1b: The electric field at the p-n junction separating electron-hole pairs
